warmup.text: In Chapter 14, Joseph tells Isaac his story: how he was caught, and how he got away. He tells it calmly, but a lot happens. Today you will reread part of it and put the events in order. Notice which event made the next one possible.

words.text: Put the feeling roots to work today. Then the spelling words: when a vowel is too quiet to hear, say a related word where that beat is strong. The vowel comes back. The council fire game uses the same trick.

reading.text: Read Chapter 14 in your book. Joseph tells his story in order, from the hunt to the cave. Follow each step. Then try the Read Like a Writer box, where one sentence skips a whole night, and finish with the Virtue Watch.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 14. The last one connects three secrets from Chapters 12, 13 and 14. Then revise your theme paragraph with the checklist, and add a second piece of evidence.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Fix the second sentence out loud.
Tap Check My Work to compare.
how.why: A comma in the right place shows the reader where one part of a sentence ends and the next begins.

do: Tap a word.
Then tap the root it belongs to.
Match all four words.
how.why: If you know the root, you can work out a word you have never seen.

do: Type the word that fits each sentence.
Open the Word Bank if you need it.
Tap Check My Words.
how.why: Putting a word back in its sentence shows you really know it.

do: Tap the correct version in each pair.
Watch for two sentences joined by only a comma.
Fix the comma splice three ways in the box.
how.why: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.

do: Say the word, then say its relative.
Find where the stress falls.
Tap a word, then tap its column.
how.why: A related word can make a quiet vowel loud again.

do: Tap your lens for today.
Reread part of Joseph's story.
Put the events in order, and ask which one made the next possible.
how.why: Rereading for order shows how one event leads to the next.
how.use: You will use this for question 1.

do: Read Chapter 14 first.
Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
For question 3, use one detail from each chapter.
how.why: These questions check what happened and what each event made harder.

do: Reread your draft with the checklist.
Add a second piece of evidence.
Explain how both pieces prove your theme.
how.why: Revising means making the proof stronger, not starting over.
how.use: Next lesson you will write the final paragraph.

do: Read what justice means.
Read the example from this week.
After you read, use the justice meter at the end of this tab.
Read the chapter introduction below.
Open your book and read Chapter 14.
Then do the Virtue Watch and the Read Like a Writer box below.

game.title: Council Fire
game.sub: This week's word game · 5 logs today
game.look: On the walk, families gather around a fire every night. In this game, each pair of related words is a log. Say each word and tap the beat you say the strongest. Get both words right and the log goes on the fire. Your fire keeps burning all week.

do: Say the first word out loud.
Tap the beat you say the strongest.
Do the same for the second word.
Tap Next log.
how.why: When a word grows, its strong beat can move. Hearing the move helps you spell the quiet vowels.

art.look: Arkhip Kuindzhi painted these patches of moonlight in a winter forest in Russia in the early 1900s. In Chapter 14, Joseph runs through the night: “The moon shone bright and I could see where I was going.”

virtue.name: justice
virtue.title: The justice meter
virtue.intro: Think about one moment from Chapter 14.
virtue.moment: The soldiers laughed about the deaths in Joseph's town. Joseph escaped. Instead of running far away, he followed the walkers and found where the same soldiers hold Naomi.
virtue.ask: How much did Joseph act for justice? Slide to show.
virtue.take: Mason's take: a lot. Joseph could have stayed far away from those soldiers. He came back to help a girl they had taken. In Chapter 13 he says, “Right now, we need to find Naomi.”
